The Humphead snapper, Lutjanus sanguineus, is a large-bodied lutjanid that supports valuable fisheries across the Indo-Pacific region. Field surveys of this species have recorded that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weigh approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams], a modest starting mass derived from the yolk reserves of pelagic eggs with a diameter similar to that observed in the star-spot snapper, Lutjanus stellatus. This initial mass reflects the small size of the fertilised ovum and the limited endogenous energy available to the lecithotrophic larva before the onset of exogenous feeding. As the larvae develop and undergo larval metamorphosis, they transition to a pelagic larval phase characterised by rapid growth. Following settlement and the juvenile stage, individuals continue to grow over several years. Maximum adult size, as recorded from extensive gillnet and hook-and-line captures throughout their range, is a fork length of 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], a dimension that places Lutjanus sanguineus among the larger members of its genus.

Reproductive maturation in female Humphead snapper has been assessed through histological examination of ovaries collected across seasonal sampling campaigns. The fork length at which 50 percent of females first exhibit vitellogenic oocytes, indicating the onset of puberty, is 51.1 centimeters [Lp = 51.1 centimeters]. Puberty in this species is therefore attained at a size equivalent to roughly half the maximum recorded fork length, a pattern common among iteroparous tropical reef fishes. The timing of this gonadal maturation is closely linked to individual growth rates, which are themselves influenced by local environmental conditions such as prey availability and water temperature. Histological sections reveal that the earliest signs of oocyte development, including cortical alveolar stage oocytes, become apparent in females once they cross this size threshold. Males, by contrast, appear to mature at a slightly smaller fork length, though quantitative studies on spermatogenic onset remain limited. The maturation schedule of Lutjanus sanguineus is consistent with that of other reef-associated lutjanids.

At a sustained water temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], conditions typical of the tropical reef environments this species inhabits, reproductive output is considerable. Each individual spawning event yields approximately 10000 to 15000 eggs per batch [N_R_i = approximately 10000 to 15000 eggs per batch], and up to 2 spawning seasons occur each year [F_R_i = up to 2 spawning seasons occur each year], resulting in an annual egg production of 2620000 eggs per year. Total lifetime egg production, given the maximum lifespan, is substantial. The high fecundity of this species is characteristic of many lutjanids, which rely on a broadcast spawning strategy to offset high rates of egg and larval mortality in the pelagic environment.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Humphead snappers has been estimated from length-weight regressions derived from a large dataset of commercially caught individuals. Using the relationship established for this species, a fish reaching the asymptotic fork length of 100 centimeters corresponds to a wet weight of 12019 grams [Wwi = 12019 grams]. This body mass represents the maximum recorded for the species and is achieved after several years of sustained growth following the juvenile phase. The length-weight relationship is highly robust across the species' geographic range, though slight regional variations have been noted, possibly attributable to differences in local prey resources or thermal regimes. Individuals weighing over 10000 grams are considered large adults and are typically the most fecund members of the population, contributing disproportionately to annual recruitment. Comparisons with other large lutjanids, such as Lutjanus johnii and Lutjanus bohar, indicate that the mass-to-length scaling in Lutjanus sanguineus is consistent with a deep-bodied, moderately compressed body shape.

Longevity data for the Humphead snapper indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 4745 days [am = approximately 4745 days] based on otolith increment analysis of individuals collected across their range at a temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C]. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of tropical reefs at 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], the oldest documented individual was recorded at approximately 4745 days, which corresponds to roughly 13 years [am = roughly 13 years]. This lifespan, measured from alevin stage through to senescence and natural death, is typical for a large, slow-growing lutjanid species. The oldest recorded individuals often show pronounced reproductive senescence, with a marked decline in fecundity and egg quality during the final years of life. Otolith microchemistry studies suggest that these long-lived individuals have experienced relatively stable thermal histories, consistent with the narrow annual temperature range of their coral reef habitats. The combination of a moderately long lifespan and high annual fecundity results in a lifetime reproductive output that can exceed several tens of millions of eggs per female, ensuring strong recruitment potential across fluctuating environmental conditions.
